Window tax was a system in force between 1697 and 1851,[a]Window tax was not introduced in Scotland until 1748.[2] in which tax on a property was based on the number of its windows.[3] It was introduced by the government of King William III at the rate of 2 shillings for houses with fewer than 10 windows, excluding cottages, 6 shillings for 10–20 windows, and 10 shillings for more than 20 windows;[4] from 1825 properties with fewer than 8 windows were exempt.[5]

The window tax was introduced to pay for the losses incurred during the great recoinage of 1696, when the silver coins then in circulation had been so clipped and worn that they were no longer viable tender, especially abroad, as their weight no longer equaled their nominal value.[6] The government needed to raise money, but the idea of a tax on income was controversial,[b]Income tax was not introduced in the UK until 1799.[7] and so, on the supposition that the more windows a habitation had, the richer its occupants must be, the window tax was introduced.[8]


Urban legends


It is widely believed that the window tax led many householders to brick up their windows to reduce their tax bill, but that is now considered to be more urban legend than fact.[1] At the very least, the number of windows that were blocked up to avoid paying the tax is often exaggerated,[5] although they were often stopped up temporarily before the periodic inspections to count windows.[4]

In similar vein, the phrase daylight robbery is popularly believed to originate with the window tax, which seems unlikely as the first recorded use of that phrase occurs in 1804, more than a hundred years after the tax was introduced.[9] It was then used in its literal sense – to describe an actual robbery that took place during daylight – in the English literary journal The Monthly Review.[10]

Introduced by King William III's government to pay for losses from the great recoinage of 1696, rates varied according to the number of windows, with exemptions for cottages and, from 1825, properties with fewer than 8 windows. Urban legends suggest it led people to brick up windows, though this is considered exaggerated. The phrase 'daylight robbery' is popularly associated with it, though its first recorded use was in 1804 in The Monthly Review to describe an actual robbery.

Генри Джон Иннс-Кер, 8-й герцог Роксбург (англ. Henry Innes-Ker, 8th Duke of Roxburghe; 24 июля 1876 — 29 сентября 1932) — шотландский аристократ, пэр, военный и придворный.


Ранняя жизнь

Генри Джон Иннс-Кер родился 24 июля 1876 года. Он был старшим сыном Джеймса Генри Роберта Иннс-Кера, 7-го герцога Роксбурга (1839—1892), и леди Энн Эмили Спенсер-Черчилль (1854—1923), четвёртой дочери Джона Спенсера-Черчилля, 7-го герцога Мальборо, который в правительстве консерваторов занимал посты лорда-президента Совета и лорда-лейтенанта Ирландии, и его жены, леди Энн Фрэнсис Вейн, дочери 3-го маркиза Лондондерри[2]. Его двоюродным братом был Уинстон Черчилль, премьер-министр Великобритании. Его младший брат, лорд Роберт Эдвард Иннс-Кер (1885—1958) женился на актрисе Хосе Коллинз[3].

Он учился в Итонском колледже и Королевском военном колледже в Сандхёрсте[4][5].


Пэрство

23 октября 1892 года, после смерти своего отца, он унаследовал титулы 8-го герцога Роксбурга, 8-го маркиза Боумонта и Кессфорда, 12-го графа Роксбурга, 8-го графа Келсо, 3-го графа Иннса, 8-го виконта Броксмута, 9-го баронета Иннса, 12-го лорда Роксбурга и 8-го лорда Кера из Кессфорда и Кавертауна[4].


Карьера

Он начал свою военную карьеру лейтенантом Королевской конной гвардии[5]. В 1895 году он получил звание второго лейтенанта 4-го батальона Аргайл-сатерлендского хайлендского полка (ополчение). В 1900 году он служил в сводном полку домашней кавалерии в Южной Африке во время Второй англо-бурской войны[6]. В 1901 марте он был назначен адъютантом герцога Корнуолла и Йорка во время его колониального турне в марте-октябре 1901 года[7]. Позднее он участвовал в Первой мировой войне, где был тяжело ранен.

Герцог стал кавалером Королевского Викторианского Ордена в феврале 1901 года[8]. Он был назначен кавалером Ордена Чертополоха в списке почестей коронации 1902 года, опубликованном 26 июня 1902 года[9], и был награждён новым королем Эдуардом VII в Букингемском дворце 8 августа 1902 года[10]. Он служил канцлером Ордена Чертополоха с 1926 до 1932 года[4].

Он служил лордом-лейтенантом Роксбургшира с 1918 года до своей смерти. В 1930 году он был назначен лейтенантом Королевской роты лучников[4].


Личная жизнь

10 ноября 1903 года[11] герцог Роксбург женился на богатой американке Мэри Гоэлет (6 октября 1878 — 26 апреля 1937), дочери миллионера из Нью-Йорка Огдена Гоэлета[12]. На момент их свадьбы она была одной из самых богатых американских наследниц с приданым в двадцать миллионов долларов, превышающим только приданое Консуэло Вандербильт[13][14]. Они жили в замке Флорс на 60 500 акрах[5], которые Мэри украсила своей собственной коллекцией произведений искусства, включая серию Гобеленов XVII века[15]. У супругов родился один сын:

 * Джордж Виктор Роберт Джон Иннс-Кер, 10-й герцог Роксбург (7 сентября 1913 — 26 сентября 1974)[16][17], его крёстным отцом был король Георг V. Среди его крестных родителей была королева-консорт Великобритании Александра[18].

Герцог Роксбург скончался 29 сентября 1932 года, и его титулы унаследовал его единственный сын, Джордж Виктор Роберт Джон Иннс-Кер, 9-й герцог Роксбург[5][17].

resultats_lens.texte_contexte: Henry John Innes-Ker, 8th Duke of Roxburghe (24 July 1876 – 29 September 1932), was a Scottish aristocrat, peer, military figure, and courtier. He was the son of James Henry Robert Innes-Ker, 7th Duke of Roxburghe, and Lady Anne Emily Spencer-Churchill, and a cousin of Winston Churchill. Educated at Eton College and the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, he inherited his titles in 1892. He served in the British Army during the Second Anglo-Boer War and World War I, where he was severely wounded.

webpage.text:
Floors Castle

Kelso, Roxburghshire

Built from 1721, for John Ker (1680-1741) who was created the 1st Duke of Roxburghe for helping to bring about the union of England with Scotland in 1706. The architect was William Adam (1689-1748) and he built the manor house incorporating the old tower house that had previously been the seat of Ker's family, the Earls of Roxburghe. In 1837, it was embellished with turrets and battlements by William Playfair, for the 6th Duke of Roxburghe. In 1903, the 8th Duke was married at Ochre Court to the American heiress Mary Goelet (1878-1937). Her $28 million fortune ensured Floors' future and she also enhanced the castle by bringing over her art and antiques from America, including the Gobelin tapestries in the ballroom and the paintings by Matisse. The castle and its 60,500-acre estate is today home to the 10th Duke and open to the public. It was here in 1986 that Prince Andrew became engaged to Sarah Ferguson.

webpage.text:
Floors Castle | Kelso | The Castles of Scotland, Coventry

Floors Castle is the massive and magnificent mansion of the Kerr Dukes of Roxburghe, with a richly decorated and sumptuous interior, set in rolling grounds with a colourful walled garden, near Kelso in the Broders in southern Scotland.

Floors Castle (© Martin Coventry)

Borders: About 1 mile north-west of Kelso, on minor roads west of A6089 or south of B6397, north of River Tweed, at Floors Castle.

Private   NT 711346   OS: 74   TD5 7SF

OPEN: Open Easter weekend, 10.30-16.00; May-Sep, daily 10.30-17.00; Oct, 10.30-15.30; last entry 60 mins before closing. Weddings and events. Plant centre.
Tel: 01573 223333   Web: www.roxburghe.net/castle  

Floors Castle (© Martin Coventry)

The largest inhabited house in Scotland, Floors Castle is a grand and imposing mansion, with a substantial towered and turreted central block with other wings and ranges, large enough in themselves to form a substantial mansion.

Floors Castle (Lang & Lang, 1913)

The building mostly dates from 1721, and was designed by William Adam for John Kerr, 1st Duke of Roxburghe, and was added to the eastern end of an old tower house. Building materials were brought from Cessford Castle. Kerr supported the Union of Parliaments of 1707 and had been made Duke of Roxburghe that same year.

Floors Castle (© Martin Coventry)

Floors Castle: before Playfair’s remodelling and extending (Neale, 1820)

In the 1830s, the house was remodelled by William Playfair for James Innes-Ker, 6th Duke of Roxburghe, with a profusion of spires and domes. There is a beautiful and well tended walled garden with fine colourful herbaceous borders, and Floors is set in attractive landscaped parkland with fine views and old trees and woods.

Floors Castle (© Martin Coventry)

Site of tower house, and ‘Fleurs’ is marked on Blaeu’s map of The Merse. This was a property of the Kerrs of Cessford, and the place was burnt by the English under the Earl of Hertford in 1545. Some of the old tower may be incorporated into Floors Castle. The family acquired the lands and property of the wealthy Kelso Abbey following the Reformation.

Floors Castle: walled garden (© Martin Coventry)

The family, now Innes-Ker and Dukes of Roxburghe, Marquis of Bowmont and Cessford, Earl of Roxburghe, Earl of Kelso, Viscount Broxmouth etc, still own Floors, and the current Duke is Guy Innes-Ker, 10th Duke of Rosburghe.

  Floors was used in the 1984 film Greystoke: the Legend of Tarzan, Lord of the Apes with Christopher Lambert.

Floors Castle (old postcard)

One story is that the house is haunted by the ghost of a gardener, who is said to be experienced – rather than seen – outside the main entrance.

Floors Castle: view towards Roxburgh (© Martin Coventry)

In the grounds is a holly tree, reputedly where James II was killed by an exploding cannon while besieging Roxburgh Castle. The apparition of a horseman has allegedly been seen riding towards the site of the old stronghold.

webpage.text:
Glasgow, Gateway to Scotland: Witness the beauty and history of these 15 majestic castles

There are few buildings more spectacular than a castle, and Scotland has an abundance of them spread across the country. Some are ruins, others in an impeccable condition, but each is impressive in its own right and well worth the trip overseas for a first-hand experience.

Travelers will discover that Glasgow is the perfect city to visit and explore the best of Scotland’s rich history, heritage and culture. And, all of the castles featured in this article are within scenic-filled driving distance from Glasgow, making the city the ideal gateway to Scotland. Once you learn the stories behind these 15 Scotland castles, you’ll be ready to plan your first or next trip!

1. Urquhart Castle

Starting with one of the greats. Perched on the banks of Loch Ness, the ruins of Urquhart Castle are an imposing sight. The castle has packed a lot of history into 1000 years: playing a key role during the Wars of Scottish Independence and being site where St Columba was said to have worked miracles in the 6th century. Located at Drumnadrochit, Inverness. Adults £9, Child £5.40. Open every day, 9.30 a.m.-8 p.m.

2. Kelburn Castle

Instantly memorable for the brightly colored murals on its walls, Kelburn certainly stands out from the more traditional castles. The original building was constructed as far back as the 13th century but had its vibrant makeover from a group of Brazilian artists in 2007. Castle aside, there is a waterfall and gorge walk to explore as well as a Secret Forest for children — a complex of paths and raised walkways with surprises at every turn. Located at Kelburn Estate and Country Centre, Fairlie, Largs, Ayrshire. Adults £9, Child/ Concession £7 (until September 2). Open every day 10 a.m.-6 p.m.

3. St. Andrews Castle

With tourists flocking to the golf courses and beaches, St. Andrews Castle may be missed by visitors. But to do so would be to miss a real gem of an experience, with an interactive trail that leads you through the visitor center and outside to the ruins of the castle. You can enjoy great views of the wild North Sea from the towers and then head underground for the real highlight: A network of hidden tunnels built by a prisoner of the castle during a failed escape. Great fun for those with a sense of adventure, not for those who suffer from claustrophobia. Located at The Scores, St. Andrews, Fife. Adult £6, Children ages 5-15 £3.60, Free entry for children under age 5. Open every day, 9.30 a.m.-5 p.m.

4. Stirling Castle

Often upstaged by its rival central belt castle in Edinburgh, Stirling is highly impressive in its own right, and peaks above the city skyline as it sits atop a rocky crag. The castle has a distinguished royal history: Mary Queen of Scots was crowned at Stirling in 1542, and Bonnie Prince Charlie unsuccessfully tried to take the castle in 1746. And, of course, it played a key role during the Wars of Scottish Independence. Today you can meet the costumed characters, enjoy a guided tour and head to the palace vaults where children can dress in period costume and play medieval instruments. Located at Castle Wynd, Stirling, Stirlingshire. Adults £15, Child £9. Open every day, 9:30 a.m.-6 p.m. (until 8 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays until the end of August).

5. Eilean Donan

Probably the most iconic — and photographed — castle in Scotland, Eilean Donan is instantly recognizable for its lochside island location and the stone bridge that connects it to the mainland. A wonderful place to simply walk around and soak up the history (not to mention the views). It had a starring role in Highlander. All together now: "There can be only one.” Located at Dornie, Kyle of Lochalsh, Highlands. Adult £7.50, Children £4. Open every day, 10 a.m.-6 p.m. (opens at 9:30 a.m. in September).

6. Dundonald Castle

It might not be the most spectacular castle, but Dundonald is one of the most underrated attractions in Ayrshire. Nestled on a hilltop above the village, there is a quietly impressive atmosphere among the old stones and the dungeon, with historic dress-up clothes and guided tours available. And, being less famous than the other castles means that there are less tourists — leaving you free to soak up the atmosphere without having to dodge selfie sticks and crying children. Located at Winehouse Yett, Dundonald, Ayrshire. Adult £5, Child £3, free entry for children under age 5. Open every day, 9:30 a.m.-5:30 p.m.

7. Dunrobin Castle

If it’s a fairy-tale castle you are looking for, then look no further. The conical spires and pristine pale stonework of Dunrobin conjure up images of princess castles from storybooks and traditional European chateaus, and are a photographer’s dream. If admiring the outside isn’t enough to keep you occupied, then there is an extensive museum to enjoy inside. Located at Golspie, Sutherland, Highlands. Adult £11.50, Child £7. Open every day, 11 a.m.-4:30 p.m.

8. Linlithgow Palace

Set beside the tranquil Linlithgow Loch, this castle has a noble history as the birthplace of Mary Queen of Scots and a retreat for many royals throughout the centuries. Modern visitors can enjoy views through the oriel windows of the king’s bedchambers, or over the loch to the Forth bridges. Located at Kirkgate, Linlithgow, West Lothian. Adult £6.00, Child £3.60, free entry for children under age 5. Open every day, 9:30 a.m.- 5:30 p.m.

9. Castle Fraser, Aberdeenshire

This five-story tower house may be recognizable to some as the backdrop from Helen Mirren’s film The Queen, with its romantic sprawling walls giving a real air of grandeur. Visitors can wander through the castle and up into the round tower, with panoramic views of the surrounding countryside. Located at Sauchen, Inverurie, Aberdeenshire. Adult £11, Concession £9.50. Open every day, 10 a.m.-4 p.m.

10. Floors Castle

This grand, sprawling castle is not only a visitor attraction but also the home of the current Duke of Roxburghe — making it the biggest inhabited castle in Scotland. Visitors can explore the collection of fine art, tapestries, grand rooms and views over the River Tweed and the Cheviot Hills beyond. Located at Roxburghe Estates Office, Kelso, Roxburghshire. Adult £11.50, Child £6.50. Open every day, 11 a.m.-5 p.m.

11. Dunvegan Castle

The Isle of Skye isn’t exactly short of beautiful attractions, but a trip to Dunvegan won’t be a waste of your time. It is still owned by the MacLeod clan, and is open to the public from April to October and has 5 acres of ornate gardens and an extensive castle to explore. On display inside the castle are a number of clan paintings, cups and treasures, as well as a collection of Bonnie Prince Charlie related items — including a lock of his hair. Located at MacLeod Estate, Dunvegan House, Dunvegan, Skye. Adult £14, Child £9. Open every day, 10 a.m.-5:30 p.m.

12. Scone Palace

As the ancient crowning place of Scottish kings and queens, history is all around you at Scone Palace. There is a magnificent palace full of artwork and tapestries, as well as beautiful gardens and grounds — complete with a star-shaped maze that should keep children (and adults) busy for a while. Located at Scone, Perthshire. Adult £12, Child £8.50. Open every day, 9:30 a.m.-5 p.m.

13. Inveraray Castle

Overlooking beautiful Loch Fyne, the equally beautiful Inveraray Castle is an idyllic setting for a romantic day out, but there is also plenty to do. Young adventurers will love the Armoury Hall, with 1,300 pieces of battle memorabilia including muskets, axes and preserved swords from the Battle of Culloden. Located at Inveraray. Adult £11, Child £8. Open every day, 10 a.m.-5:45 p.m.

14. Dunnottar Castle

The dramatically rugged setting of Dunnottar, perched on a rocky headland above the North Sea, makes it a dream location for any photographer. Liberated from the English by the Scottish knight William Wallace in 1287, it was later home to the Earls Marischal, one of the most powerful families in Scotland, but the last Earl died a bachelor in 1778 and his title died with him and the castle fell into ruins. In 1925 the castle was bought by the Pearson family, and Viscountess Lady Cowdray began a program of restoration to open the castle to the public. Children will enjoy exploring the rock pools at the sea shore. Located at Stonehaven. Adult £7, Child £3. Open every day, 9 a.m.-5:30 p.m.

15. Drumlanrig Castle

With 120 rooms, 17 turrets and four towers, this Renaissance castle is not lacking in luxury. It is set in the 120,000-acre Queensberry Estate, with mountain biking, fishing and ranger-led wildlife walks. Back in the castle there are remarkable art collections to admire — including silver, porcelain and French furniture and art (most notably Rembrandt's Old Woman Reading). And for any Outlander fans, you will note with excitement that Drumlanrig was used for filming in the second series. Located at Thornhill, Dumfries & Galloway. Adult £10, Child £6, free entry for children under age 5. Open every day, 10 a.m.-5 p.m.

metadata.title: Glasgow, Gateway to Scotland: Witness the beauty and history of these 15 majestic castles

resultats_lens.texte_contexte: Glasgow serves as a gateway to exploring 15 majestic castles in Scotland within driving distance. Notable castles include Urquhart Castle on Loch Ness with a 1000-year history tied to the Wars of Scottish Independence and St Columba; Kelburn Castle featuring vibrant murals painted by Brazilian artists in 2007; St. Andrews Castle with its hidden tunnels and views of the North Sea; and Stirling Castle, associated with Mary Queen of Scots' crowning in 1542, Bonnie Prince Charlie in 1746, and the Wars of Scottish Independence.
